title: Colouring rather than keeping time (Roy Haynes's view)
summary: Greer agrees he coloured the music while two bass players held the line, and that Duke gave him freedom.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Great drummers: who they admired and why

blocks.x: Yeah, because, you know, Roy Haynes was telling me -- you know Roy Haynes?
Roy was a good pal of mine. Roy is my man.
Well, he told me that he thought you

were the first drummer that he thought kind of freed the drummer to play more different kinds of things. But he said Jo Jones was the first drummer you heard, instead of saying ("ting-tinka") ("tinka-ting") (humming) he played (humming). He turned the beat around a little bit. But then he told me, he said, man, "Sonny Greer, a lot of times he'll be playing and the bass player will be carrying the time, Sonny won't be carrying time, he'll be back there playing colors."

Yeah, that was it. You said the word. I colored them things, you know. Of course, it wasn't too hard on me to fall in for that because we had two bass players. We had two bass players that was holding the line. The only thing I was doing was coloring. Yeah, them cats would play something, I'd color it up so it sounds good.18): I know if it sounds good to me, it will sound good to everybody else. But not over exaggerate, I mean just color.

All the guys in the band liked it. Duke loved it. That's why he give me so much freedom, you know. Because he insisted that the rhythm section kept that level. Our brass, our reeds, all bands, two out of three bands, they start out here, when they go, they've done accelerated way up top. But where we started, we were right there. And that was difficult, you know.
A guy, naturally, playing a solo, he gets over energetic and he has a tendency to turn loose. You've got to hold
it. Right away he wants to take it up to the sky. But no, we have to hold him down.
